summary: This RFC defines ARP mediation for L2VPN pseudowires whose two attachment circuits use different technologies. Normally both must match, and ARP mediation lets IP interworking handle address resolution between them.

plainLanguage.summary: Two ends speak different network languages. A translator in the middle helps them find each other's addresses.

questions: how do pes handle arp in a vpws
subtitle: How provider edge routers translate address resolution so two different kinds of links can be joined into one IP-only wire.

tldr.problem: A Layer 2 VPN normally needs the same link technology on both ends, but if only IP traffic is carried, the ends could differ. Their address resolution protocols (ARP, Inverse ARP, PPP, IPv6 Neighbor Discovery) would not understand each other.
tldr.mechanism: The Provider Edge routers intercept the local address resolution, learn the IP address of the attached customer device, signal it to the far PE over LDP, and answer the local device on behalf of the remote one using the PE's own link-layer address.
tldr.outcome: Unicast IP flows only after both customer devices have been discovered. IPv4 addresses travel in LDP signaling, while IPv6 discovery packets pass through the pseudowire and are adjusted at the edges.

facts.label: Required discovery mode
facts.value: Manual configuration of the local CE IPv4 address

today: RFC 6575 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself does not describe deployments, so this page does not either.

sections.title: Joining Different Links Carrying Only IP
sections.content:
A Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) joins two Attachment Circuits (ACs) through a pseudowire between two Provider Edge (PE) devices. Each AC connects a Customer Edge (CE) device to its PE. In a pure Layer 2 VPN, both ACs must be the same type, such as both Ethernet or both Frame Relay.

If it is known that only IP traffic will be carried, the ACs can differ, provided the PEs handle the IP transfer properly. The catch is address resolution. An Ethernet-attached IPv4 CE uses ARP, while a Frame Relay CE might use Inverse ARP (RFC 2390). If AC1 is Ethernet and AC2 is Frame Relay, ARP requests from CE1 cannot be passed on unchanged, so PE1 MUST interpret them and mediate the information with PE2 before replying.

This document calls these procedures ARP Mediation. It uses the word ARP loosely for any protocol that resolves IP addresses to link-layer addresses, including Neighbor Discovery for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: If two ends use different kinds of cables and ways of asking who is who, someone in the middle has to translate. That helper is called ARP Mediation.

sections.title: The ARP Mediation Function
sections.content:
ARP Mediation (AM) lives in the PE, so the CE devices do not notice it. A PE doing it for IPv4 MUST follow five steps:

  1. Discover the IP address of the locally attached CE.
  2. Terminate ARP and Inverse ARP requests from the CE rather than forwarding them.
  3. Send that IP address to the remote PE using pseudowire control signaling.
  4. Tell the local CE the IP address of the remote CE.
  5. Answer the local CE's ARP and Inverse ARP requests using the remote CE's IP address and the local PE's own hardware address.

For IPv6 the PE instead intercepts Neighbor Discovery and Inverse Neighbor Discovery packets from the local CE, learns the CE's IPv6 configuration from them, and forwards them over the pseudowire. Packets arriving from the remote PE are intercepted too, and may be modified to suit the outgoing AC.

The IP Layer 2 Interworking Circuit works by stripping the data link header at the ingress PE and sending the bare IP packet over the pseudowire, with or without the optional control word. If several data link headers are present, all MUST be removed. The egress PE adds the header used on its own AC.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper stands at the door, hears who is asking, passes the news along, and answers with its own name. The visitors never know a helper was there.

sections.title: Discovering IPv4 Customer Addresses
sections.content:
An interworking circuit enters a monitoring state right after configuration. It discovers the CE and sets up the pseudowire, and the two happen independently. Until both CEs are discovered and the proxy functions are complete, only broadcast and multicast IP frames cross; unicast IP datagrams are dropped. The reason is that PEs do not route, the destination address in a packet is not necessarily the attached CE, and on a broadcast link the CE's MAC address cannot be worked out from a packet's destination IP address.

A PE MUST support manual configuration of the local CE's IPv4 address, and this is the only REQUIRED mode. Configuring the remote CE's address is OPTIONAL. Automatic methods a PE MAY use:

  • Monitoring local traffic, such as link-local multicast packets.
  • Reading ARP requests from an Ethernet-style CE. Only one CE per AC is supported, so on a shared LAN the PE MUST select one.
  • Answering Inverse ARP, the typical mode for Frame Relay and ATM.
  • Proxy PPP negotiation, where the PE learns the address from the IPCP IP-Address option (0x03).
  • The Router Discovery Protocol, sending a router solicitation with a source address of zero.

Once the remote CE's address is known, the PE MUST answer ARP requests from the local CE with its own MAC address, but only for requests whose target is the remote CE's IP address. It MAY also send an unsolicited ARP, and MAY periodically ARP for the CE as a heartbeat to notice failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper first has to learn who is on its own side. It can be told directly, or it can listen to what the neighbor says. Until both sides are known, only messages for everybody get through.

sections.title: IPv6 and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
IPv4 ARP and Inverse ARP are not IP packets, so they cannot ride an IP pseudowire and MUST be handled locally, with the address signaled between PEs. IPv6 address resolution uses ICMPv6 packets, which are IP, so they can cross the pseudowire and no IPv6 address signaling is needed.

A PE that supports IPv6 MUST intercept Neighbor Discovery and Inverse Neighbor Discovery on both the AC and the pseudowire, record the IPv6 and link-layer addresses, possibly modify the packets for the egress AC type, and forward them on. It MUST learn a list of IPv6 addresses for the local CE and another for the far-end CE.

  • Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement: from the local CE they are inspected and forwarded unmodified. From the pseudowire, a source link-layer address option MUST be removed, and the PE MAY substitute one with its own AC's address. This matters on Ethernet, where the CE would otherwise have no valid link-layer address to send data to.
  • Inverse Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement: if the local AC cannot do Inverse Neighbor Discovery, the PE MUST discard the INS and answer into the pseudowire with an INA, or discard an INA and send a Neighbor Advertisement to its CE.
  • Router Solicitation and Advertisement: handled like Neighbor Solicitation, and the PE MAY lower an MTU option if the pseudowire MTU is smaller.

Duplicate Address Detection packets flow through the same way, but their source is the unspecified address, so the PE cannot learn an address from them. Pseudowires carrying both IP versions SHOULD NOT let the IPv4 and IPv6 mechanisms interact.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer kind of address question is already a normal letter, so it can travel in the mail truck as is. The helpers just fix the return address on the envelope at the far end.

sections.title: Signaling Addresses and IPv6 Capability
sections.content:
A PE advertises a CE's IPv4 address only for pseudowires of the IP Layer2 Transport type (value 0x000B from RFC 4446). The address is carried in an IP Address List TLV from RFC 5036, placed in the optional parameters of the LDP Label Mapping message. Its Length is 6, the Address Family is 1 (IPv4), and the Addresses field holds the single CE address. An all-zero address means the PE has not learned its CE's address yet.

The zero value avoids a deadlock. In Frame Relay, for example, the CE sends Inverse ARP only once the circuit is active, so a PE must be ready to advertise the pseudowire before it knows the address, then re-advertise when it does. If an address stops being valid, the PE MUST re-advertise with a null address, and unicast IPv4 stops while multicast continues. Changes can also be sent in an LDP Notification message with status code 0x0000002C, "IP address of CE".

IPv6 support is signaled with a Stack Capability interface parameter sub-TLV (Parameter ID 0x16, Length 4). Bit zero, mask 0x0001, means IPv6 stack capability. A PE supporting IPv6 MUST send it in the initial Label Mapping, and PEs use only capabilities both support. On a mismatch an operator can choose one of two behaviors:

  • Operational down: the PE does not send its mapping, or withdraws its label with status code 0x0000004A (IP Address type mismatch).
  • Fallback: the PE sends a mapping without the sub-TLV, or withdraws with status code 0x000004B (Wrong IP Address type) followed by a mapping without it.
sections.plainLanguage: The helpers phone each other to share the names they learned. If one helper has not learned a name yet, it says so with a blank, and fills it in later.

sections.title: Security and IGP Notes
sections.content:
The LDP connection between trusted PEs MUST be secured by checking incoming connections against the configured peer address and authenticating LDP messages as in RFC 5036. The pseudowire is only established if the PEs have matching configuration (PW ID, PW type and MTU), which gives some protection against mis-wiring.

Learning a CE's address can itself be a security issue. The AC is expected to be physically secured. If that is a concern, the PE MUST be configured with the CE's IP and MAC address (Ethernet), IP and DLCI or VPI/VCI (Frame Relay or ATM), or IP address only (PPP), and MUST check ARP and Inverse ARP information against that configuration. On data-plane spoofing, the PE MUST sever the connection with the local CE, tear down the pseudowire and start over.

For IPv6, Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) cannot be used across an ARP Mediation pseudowire, because it conflicts with the packet modifications. PEs MUST remove SEND options, and CEs MUST be configured to accept non-SEND packets. It is therefore suggested to use IPv6 ARP Mediation only with secure ACs.

Appendix A covers routing protocols between the CEs. OSPF should be told to treat an Ethernet link as point-to-point, RIP needs no special configuration, and IS-IS cannot be supported because it does not run over IP.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the helpers trust what they hear, the doors must be locked and the helpers check names against a list. Some fancy name tags cannot be used because the helpers change the envelopes.
